channel.title: ResearchBuzz - Transformed
channel.description: News and resources covering social media, search engines, databases, archives, and other such information collections. Since 1998.

item.title: AG’s Office Launches Tool Highlighting Local Investment in Combating Drug Crisis
item.description: State of Kentucky: “In July 2025, the Commission launched an online portal for local governments to report how settlement dollars are being used across Kentucky. Each community receiving funds must, under Kentucky law, report annually how much money they receive, what is spent, and what is being done with the money. Reports must be submitted by August 31, detailing spending during the previous fiscal year. The dashboard takes reporting from local governments, as well as reporting from the state grant funding, and makes it accessible to the public. Data on the dashboard will be updated at regular intervals and new functionalities will develop over the next several months.”

item.title: Historic Hudson Valley launches Digital Library and Collections Portal
item.description: Westfair Business Journal: “The newly launched portal helps integrate Historic Hudson Valley’s physical holdings into a unified digital resource. The archival collections feature more than 6,000 manuscripts, maps and graphics spanning the 17th through the 20th centuries.”

item.title: Windows Drops Under 60% in Global Desktop OS Share for the First Time in Years
item.description: Linuxiac: “In June 2026, StatCounter reported that Windows made up 56.55% of global desktop OS usage, dropping Microsoft’s share below 60%. This is a big change for an operating system that has shaped desktop computing for decades and usually led its competitors by a wide margin.”

item.title: Discord Goes Ban-Happy, Suspends People for Benign Images
item.description: Gizmodo: “According to a report from The Verge, Discord‘s safety system mistakenly banned over 8,000 users for images of things like chessboards and Minecraft inventories—an issue the company blamed on a bug.”

item.title: Flickr and Black Women Photographers Launch $10,000 Grant
item.description: PetaPixel: “Flickr and the organization Black Women Photographers have announced the return of their annual grant program, offering a $10,000 award to a Black female or non-binary photographer. Now in its fourth year, the initiative represents the largest grant the partnership has offered to date.”

item.title: The FCC wants to make easier for ISPs to hide junk fees
item.description: Engadget: “The Republican-led FCC is moving to modify a transparency rule that could make it much easier for internet service providers (ISPs) to charge hidden fees, according to a report by Ars Technica.”

item.title: Ohio college syllabi are going public under Senate Bill 1
item.description: Signal Ohio: “Ohio college students – or anyone with an internet connection – will soon be able to find out information about a class before ever enrolling. This fall marks the first time state institutions are required to publicly post undergraduate course syllabi under Senate Bill 1. The sweeping state law overhauling how higher education operates passed last year.”

item.title: Kentucky Secretary Of State Launches Time Capsule Project
item.description: State of Kentucky: “The Kentucky Time Capsule Project invites Kentuckians from every corner of the state to contribute their voices, stories, photographs, artwork, and hopes for the future. Those interested in submitting can do so through the Secretary of State’s website at sos.ky.gov.”

item.title: How Canadian scientists are stepping up in the race to save climate data
item.description: Canada’s National Observer: “At Ocean Networks Canada in Victoria, BC, Kate Moran was ready with big questions for a planned call with her colleague on Canada’s opposite coast. The two ocean scientists were discussing responses to a massive, unexpected problem: the US National Science Foundation (NSF), under the Trump administration, had just announced a plan to dismantle and remove infrastructure collecting key climate data in the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans.”

item.title: New Mexico regulators announce 16 community solar projects are online, generating power
item.description: Source New Mexico: “The New Mexico Public Regulation Commission on Wednesday announced that more than one-third of its planned 47 community solar power projects are operational. When fully built out, the community solar program is expected to deliver 200 megawatts of renewable energy in areas serviced by Public Service Company of New Mexico, Southwestern Public Service Company and El Paso Electric, the PRC announced.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Big Tech Is Now Targeting Native American Land for Massive Data Centers
item.description: New York Times: This link goes to a gift article. “The dizzying expansion of data centers to power artificial intelligence has communities in Republican and Democratic states feeling blindsided as citizens and local governments are forced to grapple with noise, water and energy concerns. That division may be even more palpable on Native lands, where outside exploitation has a long and ugly history and where technology companies see a chance for rapid development that gets past the red tape impeding projects elsewhere.”

item.title: Data center fights pit social values, democracy and capitalism against each other
item.description: The Conversation: “A look at some of the forces at play around these projects reveals the deep issues they raise. The fights about data centers can often take the form of collisions between companies and community members. But they also reflect conflict about social values, democratic systems and capitalist interests.”

item.title: UK guts planning red tape so datacenters can bypass the neighbors faster
item.description: The Register: “Reform of the Planning and Infrastructure Act 2025 aims to cut a year off the approval process for Nationally Significant Infrastructure Projects (NSIPs) in England and Wales – a category that now includes datacenters.”

item.title: Even banks and hyperscalers are now sounding the alarm about the AI bubble
item.description: The Register: “The Bank for International Settlements, often referred to as ‘the central bank for central banks’, said in a report at the end of June that it was worried the AI bubble was nigh on to popping and taking the global economy with it. Oracle, the hyperscaler with arguably the largest exposure to the AI bubble, has lost more than 40 percent of its share value in the past month and recently outlined all the ways it might suffer if this whole AI thing doesn’t pan out.”

item.title: Georgia utility regulators greenlight probe into data center costs
item.description: Georgia Recorder: “The Georgia Public Service Commission approved an investigation into whether Georgia Power’s industrial customers who are heavy energy consumers, like data centers, are shifting some costs to residential customers.”

item.title: Virginia DEQ Uses AI to Speed Environmental Permit Reviews
item.description: State Tech Magazine: “The Virginia Department of Environmental Quality is using artificial intelligence to streamline environmental permitting, positioning the technology to help agency staff manage a growing workload while continuing to shorten review times.”

item.title: As AI boom reaches Massachusetts, state lawmakers push for strict data center rules
item.description: Daily Hampshire Gazette: “State lawmakers have proposed a change to the Legislature that would hold data centers responsible for their environmental and financial impact on communities, as developers continue to eye Massachusetts as an ideal location.”

item.title: New State AI safety and transparency measure signed into law
item.description: The Times Weekly: “Senate Bill 315 requires large frontier AI developers – such as ChatGPT and Claude – to assess catastrophic risks, report critical safety incidents, undergo independent third-party audits and establish whistleblower protections for employees raising safety concerns.”

item.title: Inside xAI: 100-hour weeks, boardrooms named ‘Judgment Day,’ and a culture of fear
item.description: San Francisco Standard: “By the time he got sick enough to go to the emergency room, he had been working 100-hour weeks for several months. But a 26-year-old xAI employee, who spoke with The Standard on condition of anonymity, knew the work didn’t stop. Texts he received from his boss while he was in the ER waiting room confirmed it. That was when he knew the culture at Elon Musk’s AI company had crossed from intense to something else entirely.”

item.title: Google will now disclose which ads are made with AI
item.description: TechCrunch: “While Google prohibits misleading and deceptive ads, an ad can still leverage AI to create some type of synthetic or digitally altered content. Until now, that’s something Google only required election ads to disclose.”

item.title: AI-related copyright losses cost celebrities up to ¥4.5 billion, study says
item.description: Japan Times: “Over 43,000 artificial-intelligence deepfakes that used celebrities’ likenesses without their consent were created over a two-month period last year, leading to copyright losses of up to ¥4.5 billion, a nonprofit rights group has found.”

item.title: Italy privacy watchdog fines Character.AI owner over age-check failures
item.description: Reuters: “Italy’s data protection authority fined Character Technologies, the U.S.-based owner ​of generative AI platform Character.AI for ‌breaches of data protection rules, it said on Thursday in a statement. The service ​allows users, including minors, to chat ​with AI-generated virtual characters.”

item.title: AI-human relationships are real and come with real consequences, researchers find
item.description: Northeastern University: “Prolonged interaction with AI chatbots can lead people to develop an emotional dependence on the technology, potentially alienating them from human relationships, said Andreia Sofia Teixeira, an associate professor at Northeastern University London in the Network Science Institute who co-authored the recent work. As a growing number of lawsuits claim chatbots’ role in people’s deaths, the new research underscores how being caught in an echo chamber with a sycophantic tool can potentially spell disaster for the most vulnerable.”

item.title: Texting a stranger works better to fight loneliness than talking to an AI chatbot
item.description: PsyPost: “New research published in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology reveals that texting a random human peer each day successfully reduces loneliness over time, while chatting with a highly supportive artificial intelligence program does not. The findings suggest that building real social connections requires more than simply receiving simulated empathy.”

item.title: When It Comes to Energy Use, AI Agents Could Make Chatbots Look Like Pocket Calculators
item.description: Gizmodo: “A new research paper from the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology set out to quantify the ‘hidden costs’ of AI agents, and found they can consume up to 136.5 times more energy per query than generative AI models.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Maritime Museum of B.C. launches redesigned global maritime history database
item.description: CHEK News: “The Maritime Museum of British Columbia has unveiled a completely redesigned version of Nauticapedia, transforming the long-running maritime history database into what the museum says is one of the world’s largest digital collections dedicated to marine history.”

item.title: It’s Now Imperative That You Copy That Floppy
item.description: Hackaday: “Copy That Floppy! only briefly touches on the most ideal situation — that is, buying a USB floppy drive and making copies of the bog standard 3.5 inch disks you might come across. It then moves right on into more advanced topics, such as interfacing with less common drive types, how to safely clean floppies, and the use of advanced tools such as Greaseweazle to analyze captured disk images.”

item.title: Google Search hit an all-time usage record yesterday
item.description: 9to5 Google: “VP of Product over Google Search, Robby Stein, and SVP of Knowledge & Information, Nick Fox, took to Twitter/X today to confirm that Google Search hit an all-time usage high this week. Specifically, Fox says, ‘right after’ the winning goal was scored during the Argentina vs Egypt match.”

item.title: Google appeals Indian ruling over its ads platform, citing consumer harm
item.description: Reuters: “Google has challenged an Indian ​court ruling that it infringed on a company’s trademark rights by allowing rivals to use its ‌name as an advertising keyword, arguing the decision will hurt consumers, documents reviewed by Reuters show.”

item.title: How to Turn Interactive Maps into Vector Graphics
item.description: Maps Mania: “Map2SVG is an interactive web application built on MapLibre that lets you select any area on a map and export it as a layered SVG file. Simply navigate to the location you want, draw either a rectangle or a custom polygon around the area of interest, and click Export.”

item.title: BBC A “Disinfectant” To Disinformation On YouTube & X/Twitter, Says New Boss
item.description: Deadline: “BBC director general Matt Brittin has said that the British broadcaster will double down on YouTube and X/Twitter to counter the tidal wave of disinformation online. Brittin may have spent the majority of his career at Google, but it did not stop him from acknowledging that YouTube is a breeding ground for deliberately deceptive information.”

item.title: American fitness influencer drowns in Samut Prakan
item.description: Bangkok Post: “A 32-year-old American fitness influencer drowned on Tuesday evening after he jumped into a lake at a housing estate in Samut Prakan province, where police also found he had vandalised his rented luxury house…. He was identified as Connor Michael Murphy, a Texas-born fitness influencer and bodybuilder.”

item.title: Do Smart Glasses Have a Surveillance Problem?
item.description: Vogue Business: “Big Tech has been borrowing from fashion’s playbook to improve its image, and the new Kylie partnership and glasses line launch is its biggest pivot to fashion and culture yet. Beneath the question of whether Jenner can finally make Meta’s smart glasses cool, there’s a much more challenging question for Meta and its rivals. Is recruiting fashion’s most influential tastemakers enough to normalize a product that fundamentally makes consumers so uneasy?” No.

item.title: Moody Bible Institute breach leaves 2.3M accounts needing salvation, says cyber expert
item.description: The Register: “Data on more than 2.3 million people associated with Moody Bible Institute (MBI) has been exposed online after the Christian college was targeted by ShinyHunters. The attack was first disclosed by MBI in June, and the extortion crew later leaked the stolen data. Have I Been Pwned has since added the cache to its breach notification database, putting a figure on the number of exposed accounts.”

item.title: Up to 10 years in jail and up to Dh10 million in fines under new UAE Cultural Heritage Law
item.description: Gulf News: “The UAE has approved a new federal Cultural Heritage Law introducing prison terms of up to 10 years and fines of as much as Dh10 million for offences against the country’s cultural heritage, as part of a comprehensive framework aimed at protecting archaeological sites, historical assets and digital heritage for future generations.”

item.title: Plutarch’s ancient advice for how to be happier online
item.description: The Conversation: “Plutarch’s counsel for us today would not be to turn our devices off. This is not socially possible for most people, given the changed nature of work and leisure. Yet recent legal findings in the US, as well as growing research on the effects of social media use, especially on young people, underscore that algorithm-driven social media does not promote, and can negatively effect, individual wellbeing.”

item.title: Designing a 4D Digital Archive for Ikebana
item.description: Ishiguro Laboratory, The University of Tokyo: Ikebana is the Japanese art of flower arranging. “We proposed the design of a 4D digital viewing system for archiving the embodied creation process of Ikebana. Using twenty-two synchronized fixed cameras and a grasses type eye tracker, our system captures full-body motion, the evolving flower arrangements, and gaze behavior.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: The Reports of Jim Carrey’s Death are a Failure Mode
item.description: Tane Piper: “On the 29th June 2026 – if you searched for Jim Carrey on Google, you would have been presented with a Knowledge Panel stating that he had died the previous day. The panel included a date of death and a biography written in the past tense.”

item.title: Data center critics flood Alaska land managers with opposition to North Slope project
item.description: Alaska Current: “Opposition is pouring in against a large data center and power plant proposed for Alaska’s North Slope, as Gov. Mike Dunleavy’s administration considers whether to approve a 50-year lease of state land to the project’s developer. More than 500 public comments were received before a preliminary deadline set by the Alaska Department of Natural Resources, according to copies of the messages released by the agency.”

item.title: Musk promised his data center would reuse water. That’s now stalled.
item.description: Politico: “The company announced it was stopping work on the water recycling plant in April, a month after its CEO touted it in a meeting with President Donald Trump. Now, Memphis residents are worried about their drinking water in an episode legal experts and scientists say is indicative of a broader pitfall of the data center boom.”

item.title: Cheyenne Won’t Take Data Center Wastewater After Meta Contractor Contaminated System
item.description: Cowboy State Daily: “The announcement was made by the Board of Public Utilities (BOPU) on Thursday in conjunction with naming the Meta company as the source of the initial contamination. It also comes more than four months after the Meta company — which is building a huge $800 million data center in south Cheyenne — disrupted the city’s reclaimed wastewater system with a rare bacterial contaminant.”

item.title: Brown Professor Suspects Majority of His Class Used AI to Cheat
item.description: Inside Higher Ed: “His welfare economics class typically attracted up to 30 students, but this spring he taught 86—an increase he attributes to the promised take-home exams. When the midterm came along, the average score was 96 percent.”

item.title: OpenAI to publicly release GPT-5.6 AI models, ending government-requested limits
item.description: CNBC: “OpenAI said it will publicly release its GPT-5.6 Sol, Terra and Luna models on Thursday, roughly two weeks after the artificial intelligence company limited the rollout to a ‘small group of trusted partners’ at the request of the U.S. government.”

item.title: ‘A massive screw-up’: China hardliners take aim at Commerce Department official
item.description: Politico: “Beijing may have mistakenly accessed thousands of high-end U.S. computer chips due to an oversight by the Trump administration in May of last year. The government hasn’t updated its blacklist of foreign firms barred from receiving American technology in months. Export license applications are piling up without approvals. And rulemaking by the agency is at its slowest pace in two decades, a POLITICO analysis of federal register rule notices found.”

item.title: Jay data center developer sought to give Janet Mills ‘cover’ for key veto, emails show
item.description: Maine Monitor: “Gov. Janet Mills’ office worked closely with the developer behind a stalled Jay data center project who solicited local letters of support that would give her ‘cover’ to veto a statewide data center ban, according to emails obtained by the Bangor Daily News.”

item.title: Legislature votes to eliminate $250 million in AI data center tax credits
item.description: New Jersey Globe: “Assemblyman Andrew Macurdy (D-Summit) hailed the overwhelming bipartisan support for legislation eliminating $250 million in uncommitted tax credits for artificial intelligence and data center projects after the General Assembly approved the measure by a 74-4 vote on June 30.”

item.title: Reddit to combat AI with more AI
item.description: Engadget: “To combat the rise of AI-generated content on Reddit, the social media platform is using its own AI tools, according to a post on its website. Reddit said its automated systems resulted in blocking 23 million spam views a day, catching roughly 25,000 posts and comments per day and revoking close to two million inauthentic votes a day.”

item.title: Midjourney pushes to expose studios’ own AI practices in copyright fight
item.description: Mashable: “Midjourney is attempting to turn the tables on the Hollywood studios suing it for copyright infringement, asking a federal judge to compel Disney, Universal, and Warner Bros. Discovery to disclose their internal use of artificial intelligence, according to a Variety report published this week.”

item.title: Secret Claude tracker shocks users after Anthropic’s anti-surveillance stance
item.description: Ars Technica: “Anthropic quickly removed a tracker secretly monitoring Claude Code users in China after a security researcher exposed the hidden code and condemned the spyware-like tracking as a ‘serious breach of user trust.'”

item.title: Voters of both parties want tighter AI regulation, poll finds
item.description: NBC News: “An overwhelming majority of likely voters want powerful AI systems to undergo mandatory formal safety reviews before they are released to the public, according to a new survey about Americans’ views on AI, going further than the existing Trump administration policy of opt-in reviews for new advanced models.”

item.title: Anthropic’s Claude Science bets on workflow, not a new model, to win over scientists
item.description: TechCrunch: “Anthropic introduced Claude Science on Tuesday, an AI workbench that gives scientists one environment to do computational research, sparing them the hassle of bouncing between databases, pipelines, and tools.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Using AI to Let History Speak About Bank Runs
item.description: Federal Reserve Bank of New York: “In a new paper, we use large language models (LLMs) to extract information on bank runs from millions of digitized historical newspaper pages, creating the most comprehensive database of bank runs in U.S. history. Every bank run episode that we identify is documented on a companion website where users can browse and examine individual episodes, and read the original newspaper articles.”

item.title: The AI that spawned MechaHitler and deepfake porn puts on a suit to become legal advisor and Excel jockey
item.description: The Register: “…the recently renamed Eloncorp known as SpaceXAI says Grok, now in version 4.5, has cleaned up its act, wiped its browser history, covered up the swastikas, and is ready to take on more serious endeavors such as tending to your legal quandaries, fiddling in Microsoft Excel, and generating code.” I trust that about as much as I trust Graham Platner.

item.title: Despite ‘misgivings,’ judge approves Elon Musk’s $1.5M SEC settlement
item.description: TechCrunch: “A judge has approved a $1.5 million penalty levied against Elon Musk that will settle a U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission lawsuit despite having ‘significant misgivings’ about it.”

item.title: “Knockoff” browser add-on filters junk brands from Amazon results
item.description: Boing Boing: “Knockoff is ‘Amazon, without the knockoffs’: a browser extension for Chrome that filters out the gibberish factory brands that are typically favoried over quality products in the online retailer’s search results.”

item.title: Trump’s Department of Education Celebrates ‘American History’ With Old Photo From U.K.
item.description: Gizmodo: “The U.S. Department of Education posted a historic photo to Facebook on Wednesday proclaiming, ‘American history is worth learning.’ The image shows women in clothes from the early 20th century demanding the right to vote. It’s an inspiring thing to behold. But it’s not American history. The photo is from the United Kingdom.”

item.title: Can YouTube gamify its videos? Two ‘Mario Kart’ fans pulled it off.
item.description: Tubefilter: “A playable version of Rainrow Road has come to YouTube. The notable Mario Kart level is featured in a video that utilizes YouTube’s 360-degree format to turn the platform’s video player into an interactive experience.”

item.title: Members of a sexual predator network on Telegram tried to hide their crimes with code words
item.description: Associated Press: “They called themselves the ‘German driving school for experts,’ but prosecutors say the true purpose of their Telegram chats was to brag about the women they raped and share tips about how to drug them.”

item.title: Cash App parent settles states’ probe over fraud protections for $45 million
item.description: Reuters: “State attorneys general ‌involved in the investigation said they had found that Block misled users with advertising that falsely implied that Cash App offered protections akin to a bank including cutting-edge fraud detection. Block denied wrongdoing.”

item.title: @CatsOnACouch Instagram Creator Barred from JD Vance Event Sues, Alleges Violation of First Amendment Rights
item.description: ACLU: “Amanda McGonigle, creator of the social media accounts @CatsOnACouch, filed suit today against the U.S. Secret Service and the Executive Office of the President, alleging that she was barred from an official government event because of her social media content criticizing the vice president.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: From torn doll to prisoner art: Digital archive opens Majdanek to the world
item.description: Ynet News: “A new digital archive gives free access to rare documents, artwork, photographs and personal belongings from the Majdanek, Bełżec and Sobibór death camps, preserving Holocaust history and supporting research, education and remembrance.”

item.title: Google announces August 12 event for Pixel 11 and Pixel Watch 5
item.description: 9to5 Google: “Made by Google 2026 is officially taking place on Wednesday, August 12. This is a week earlier compared to last year, with Google once again opting for an earlier Pixel hardware unveil.”

item.title: DuckDuckGo Browser can now block video ads, including YouTube’s
item.description: Engadget: “DuckDuckGo announced that it can now block most video ads, particularly those on YouTube, when a video is playing in its browser.”

item.title: Elon Musk’s bid to set aside Twitter fraud verdict rejected by US judge
item.description: Reuters: “A federal judge on Monday ​rejected Elon Musk’s bid to void a jury verdict finding that the world’s richest person defrauded Twitter investors by trying to drive ‌down the social media company’s stock price after agreeing to a $44 billion takeover.”

item.title: FIFA is investigating an incident between a fan and streamer IShowSpeed at a World Cup match
item.description: Associated Press: “FIFA said Tuesday it is investigating an incident involving streamer and YouTuber IShowSpeed with a fan in the stands during the World Cup match between Argentina and Cape Verde on Friday.”

item.title: Chicago National Archives Closure Will Be Loss For Historians, Researchers, Even Deep-Sea Divers
item.description: Block Club Chicago: “The National Archives and Records Administration plans to close its Chicago facility, a sprawling building on the Southwest Side that houses transcripts from the Trial of the Chicago 7, maritime records for the Great Lakes region and documents on tribal nations.”

item.title: Russia faces challenges trying to jam Starlink in Ukraine
item.description: France 24: “Footage reportedly shows Ukrainian forces destroying a Russian system deployed to jam Starlink. The satellite network, which is notoriously difficult to jam, has become crucial for providing high-speed internet access to Ukraine.”

item.title: Victims of 23andMe data breach to get $47m payout, judge rules
item.description: BBC: “Victims of a 2023 data hack at genetics testing company 23andMe are set to receive a multi-million payout from the firm. A California bankruptcy court judge ruled on Tuesday that Chrome Holding, which last year took control of 23andMe after its bankruptcy, should pay out $46.75m (£35m) in compensation.”

item.title: Police arrests 5,800 suspects in global anti-fraud crackdown
item.description: Bleeping Computer: “Law enforcement agencies have arrested 5,811 suspects and seized $293 million in illicit assets in a global anti-fraud operation spanning 97 countries.”

item.title: Louisiana doubles money available to nonprofits for conservation work
item.description: Louisiana Illuminator: “Louisiana has doubled the state money available for nonprofit groups to preserve and restore public lands of historic, environmental or recreational importance. Louisiana Outdoors Forever was allotted $2 million by the state legislature for the 2027 grant application cycle, which starts this week. That’s up from $1.07 million in 2026 and the largest amount set aside for the program since it began in 2022.”

item.title: Over 3,500 historical and cultural monuments digitized in Tajikistan
item.description: Asia+: “More than 3,500 historical and cultural monuments in Tajikistan have been digitized as part of a nationwide effort to update the State Register of protected heritage sites, according to the Agency for the Protection of Historical and Cultural Heritage under the Government of Tajikistan.”

item.title: Researchers install 3D-printed seawall tiles to support coastal protection and marine life
item.description: Florida International University: “The system uses modular, interlocking tiles that can be attached to existing seawalls. Each tile is robotically printed and designed with grooves, ridges, crevices and small pools that create more complex surfaces for marine organisms to attach, shelter and grow.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Dealing with antisemitism and Holocaust distortion on social media
item.description: University of Duisburg-Essen and machine-translated from German: “At the heart of the program is an approximately 15-minute online game that immerses participants in a realistic social media environment. There, they encounter antisemitic and Holocaust-distorting content in the same form as it is disseminated on social networks. Players take on the role of trainees in a resistance movement and analyze posts, comments, and digital communication patterns to identify antisemitic content and understand its mechanisms of dissemination.” The game is available in both English and German.

item.title: Ex Situ
item.description: Spotted in my Calishat Snaps: I would guess from from the GitHub page that it launched 3-4 months ago. Also from the Github page: “Museums across Europe and North America hold hundreds of thousands of artifacts whose provenance — where they came from, under what circumstances — remains buried in institutional databases, invisible to researchers and the public. Ex Situ makes this visible: not by duplicating institutional data, but by indexing the relationships between origin sites and destination collections as a spatial commons — connective tissue between archives that were never designed to speak to each other.”

item.title: New portal ‘Pokkhi’ maps Assam’s birdlife with 372 species in two languages
item.description: Assam Tribune: “A new digital initiative, ‘Pokkhi’ was officially launched on Sunday to document and showcase the rich avian biodiversity of Assam…. It currently features carefully-curated Assamese and English common names of 372 species, high-quality field photographs, IUCN conservation status, descriptions, and identification guides.”

item.title: Google Voice now offers paid tiers with call recording & Gemini for personal accounts
item.description: 9to5 Google: “Historically, Google Voice’s paid offerings were meant for enterprise customers, but Google is now letting you upgrade to a paid calling experience without needing a Workspace subscription.”

item.title: ExtraEmily’s suspension leads to calls to ban “streaming and driving”
item.description: Tubefilter: “After a high-profile streamer’s suspension, members of the Twitch community are calling for a rule change that would curb a dangerous epidemic of distracted driving. ExtraEmily (whose real name is Emily Xuechun Zhang) earned a temporary ban after she nearly crashed her car during one of her streams.”

item.title: Google Maps leads drivers astray onto rough forest roads near Payson
item.description: Arizona’s Family: “Gila County Sheriff’s Office posted on Sunday that multiple vehicles got stuck near Forest Service Road 64 and Forest Service Road 198, roughly 20 miles northeast of Payson. Google Maps reportedly rerouted drivers onto Forest Service Road 64 from Highway 260, causing a traffic blunder. Deputies say the drivers got stuck due to bad road conditions and two-way traffic on a one-way road.”

item.title: India gives WhatsApp three days to defend username rollout amid security fears
item.description: The Register: “India has asked WhatsApp to explain why it should not face regulatory action after it announced the global rollout of a new usernames feature amid fears that the new feature could lead to increased cyberattacks.”

item.title: French antitrust watchdog orders Meta to resume talks with media groups over publishing fees
item.description: Reuters: “France’s competition authority on Wednesday ordered Meta Platforms to put forward a payment plan and resume talks with French media groups that are seeking a year of unpaid fees for the use of their content online.”

item.title: Google is testing a webcam CAPTCHA that scans your hand, but it’s already been bypassed using a photo
item.description: TechSpot: “Google is working on a new kind of challenge to improve its reCAPTCHA system, using biometric identification to confirm that the user is indeed human. The new method is officially named ‘hand gesture verification’ (HGV), and, according to early testing, is mostly useless.”

item.title: Two Long Lost Commodore PET Adventures Recovered After 45 Years
item.description: Games That Weren’t: “The original Commodore PET editions of Brian Cotton’s Catacombs and Goblin Towers, published by Supersoft back in 1981, have been recovered after being considered lost for around 45 years thanks to Marcel Lansing.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Google AI Overviews give ‘incredibly worrying’ prominence to suicide method
item.description: Press Gazette: “Google queries about the death of former Love Island presenter Caroline Flack’s brother this week have prominently displayed details about his suicide in AI summaries at the top of search results pages.”

item.title: Now we’re getting AI fake news complaining about how AI fake news is the death of real news
item.description: NiemanLab: “Did 47 Alabama newspapers die on a single day and no one noticed? (Hint: No, they didn’t.)” Crazy read.

item.title: “Ban! Ban! Ban!”: Data-center discontent reaches western Massachusetts
item.description: The Shoestring: “An explosive growth in demand for resources, primarily power and water, needed to fuel AI data centers is being met with strong local opposition to these projects. Western Massachusetts is leading that movement in the Bay State, turning up to protest proposed projects both big and small.”

item.title: Big Tech data centers are driving up power bills at America’s Rust Belt factories
item.description: Reuters: “For years, electricity costs for the Belden Brick Company in Sugarcreek, Ohio, had been relatively stable. Last year, they surged by 90% — largely because of rising power demand from data centers in the region.”

item.title: OpenAI might give a 5 percent stake to the US government
item.description: Mashable: “According to a new report from the Financial Times, OpenAI, which is currently valued at $854 billion, is currently in early talks to give the U.S. government a five percent stake in the company.”

item.title: Governor Stein Announces AI Strategic Roadmap to Protect and Better Serve North Carolinians, Prepare Workers, and Strengthen Economy
item.description: State of North Carolina: “Governor Josh Stein’s North Carolina AI Leadership Council released the AI Strategic Roadmap, a guide with strategic goals and principles to address the potential impact of AI on how people live and work.”

item.title: New Mexico lawmakers announce proposed statewide moratorium on data centers
item.description: Source New Mexico: “Several Democratic state lawmakers on Thursday announced they intend to introduce legislation in next year’s legislative session to create a statewide moratorium on ‘large-scale’ data centers.”

item.title: Big tech has suddenly flipped on the AI jobs wipeout scenario
item.description: Wall Street Journal: “The sentiment change isn’t limited to tech leaders: A survey by EY-Parthenon found that the percentage of CEOs who believe AI investments will result in significant reductions in head count fell from around 46% in January 2025 to just 20% this May.”

item.title: Google’s AI buildout drove 37% increase in electricity use in 2025
item.description: Ars Technica: “Google reported that its annual electricity consumption rose by 37 percent in 2025—the largest increase in the company’s history as Silicon Valley’s AI data center buildout continues. But the tech giant says it kept operational carbon emissions down by continuing to purchase massive amounts of clean energy.”

item.title: Tilly Norwood, AI ‘actor’ denounced by actors union, to star in feature film
item.description: NBC News: “The feature film will be a comedy-drama called ‘Misaligned,’ and it will star Tilly Norwood in a ‘hybrid production with traditional film and TV professionals — such as directors, writers and editors — working alongside AI specialists, with AI training and mentorship built into the production itself,’ the company said.”

item.title: When AI hurts people, who’s to blame? Global experts grapple with accountability
item.description: United Nations: “Who is legally responsible when Artificial Intelligence causes harm? The issue took centre stage on Tuesday – day two of the first ever UN summit on AI governance, where leading experts warned of mounting evidence of human rights violations linked to the revolutionary technology.”

item.title: A new attack uses a BioShock-style puzzle to convince AI browsers they’re not in the real world
item.description: TechSpot: “Researchers from LayerX recently unveiled BioShocking, a new type of vulnerability designed to target AI-powered browsers capable of executing autonomous tasks on the open web. The security firm explained that BioShocking can ‘game’ an AI-based browser, causing the system to execute malicious instructions after effectively bypassing its intended security guardrails.”

item.title: Google AI Overviews Study Finds Lost Clicks Weren’t Lower Quality
item.description: Search Engine Journal: “An updated AI Overviews experiment finds no measurable difference in bounce rates, time on site, or returns to search between clicks with and without summaries.”

item.title: COrigami – an AI-based Origami Design Tool
item.description: Origami by Michał Kosmulski: “I’m very excited to announce a paper I have co-authored: COrigami: An AI Pipeline for Co-Designing Flat-Foldable Visually Recognisable Origami. It introduces COrigami, a first of its kind AI-based origami design tool, capable of generating origami crease patterns and simulating their folded look, including simple shaping, starting from a textual description.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: The Plains to Peaks Collective Launches a New Discovery Platform
item.description: Wyoming State Library: “The Colorado State Library, in partnership with the Wyoming State Library, is excited to announce the launch of a brand-new Plains to Peaks Collective site (plains2peaks.org) for searching historic collections across Colorado and Wyoming.”

item.title: Tinfoil Pigeons
item.description: Spotted in my RSS feeds: From the About section on the front page: “Every airliner, cargo hauler, helicopter and suspiciously quiet turboprop broadcasts its position over ADS-B, and our scope listens. Enter a postcode or town — anywhere in the world — or use your location, and the flights overhead appear as blips, sweep after sweep, exactly where they really are.”

item.title: California releases CalEnviroScreen 5.0 to identify and prioritize pollution-burdened communities, announces preliminary disadvantaged communities designation
item.description: State of California: “The Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment (OEHHA) today released CalEnviroScreen 5.0, an update to the state’s mapping tool that identifies communities hardest hit by multiple pollution sources. Combining data from multiple environmental, health and socioeconomic indicators, the state has used CalEnviroScreen to focus resources and environmental protection actions where they are needed most.”

item.title: Fabrice Canel, Longtime Bing Search Leader, Retires From Microsoft
item.description: Search Engine Journal: “Canel led the Bing team responsible for crawling and indexing the web, and he was closely associated with Bing Webmaster Tools. He also became the public face of IndexNow, the open protocol Microsoft Bing announced with Yandex in 2021 for notifying search engines about new and updated pages.”

item.title: Google Maps is restoring the names of locations in Poland that were changed to offensive alternatives
item.description: 9to5 Google: “Polish news network TVPWorld reported on the matter, with examples including the Presidential Palace being renamed ‘Hooligans’ Palace,’ the Warsaw Uprising Museum becoming ‘Museum of the Third Reich Uprising,’ and the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier becoming ‘Tomb of the Known SS Soldier.’ Screenshots of some of the altered names were shared on social media.”

item.title: Wordle, but for art history—Anthropeum turns the Met Museum into an online game
item.description: Scientific American: “Armchair art historians, rejoice: there’s a free online daily game just for you. Called Anthropeum, the game involves guessing where and when various artifacts from New York City’s Metropolitan Museum of Art come from.”

item.title: The Human Story of the Open Web
item.description: Jeffrey Zeldman: “The new digital landowner class can also take away our favorite software, or change it in ways to which we never consented. The answer to this destruction of our shared digital commons by a handful of billionaires is the same as it has always been: own your content on the open web (your domain on a server, like mine on this one), and replace proprietary software with open source alternatives.”

item.title: If you use Google, you’re training its AI. Here’s how to opt out.
item.description: TechCrunch: “Consider this a belated PSA: A recent change to Google’s privacy settings is allowing the company to store more of your data, including media such as ‘images, files, and audio and video recordings,’ to improve its AI models. In other words, if you upload any media to Google’s Search services, it’s being used to train AI unless you opt out.”

item.title: Musk’s X poses “serious risk to Americans’ privacy,” advocates warn FTC
item.description: Ars Technica: “Ahead of a July 2 deadline to submit public comments, advocates are warning the Federal Trade Commission that it must keep close watch over Elon Musk’s X and firmly reject a recent bid to end the agency’s ongoing audits of the platform’s data handling.”

item.title: Threads’ ubiquitous Mr Beast spam is part of a massive crypto scam network
item.description: Engadget: “A spam account replies to a popular post with a nonsensical phrase and a low-quality screenshot of the British newspaper The Times featuring a fictitious story about Mr Beast. There’s usually a second, seemingly random, image — often a bouquet of flowers with an iPhone. The formula has some minor variations, but these posts are absolutely everywhere. Like so much spam on social media, it’s part of a massive crypto scam.”

item.title: There May Be Three Times as Many Insect Species as Previously Thought
item.description: University of Connecticut: “Most experts have currently accepted an estimate of about 6 million insect species, an appraisal that has stood for the last 40 years. But the new count, which used genetic information for 1.6 million individual tropical insects, a census of a highly diverse group of parasitic wasps in Costa Rica, and statistical strategies, conservatively estimates the total number of insect species at closer to 14 to 20 million.”

item.title: Could the clean energy revolution be powered by wastewater?
item.description: Northeastern University: “The researchers found that enough magnesium, lithium, uranium, titanium, fluorine and silicon could be recovered from wastewaters to meet at least one-tenth of each resource’s projected demand in the international clean energy sector.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: New archives bring New Brunswick’s hidden queer history online
item.description: CBC: “The Queer Heritage Initiative of New Brunswick has launched a new website this week, bringing together more than a decade of archival work documenting LGBTQ+ life across the province.”

item.title: Vaccination rates in Texas schools have been dropping. Look up the latest vaccination rates in your district.
item.description: Texas Tribune: “Each school year, Texas public school districts and private schools report to the state vaccination rates for each immunization required to attend kindergarten and 7th grade. The state publishes spreadsheets with information from these reports. The Texas Tribune has made this publicly available data easily searchable. Find those coverage rates for the 2025-26 school year with the change from the previous year below.”

item.title: NYC Department of City Planning Launches NYC Language Explorer, a New Interactive Tool Mapping Languages Spoken Across the Five Boroughs
item.description: City of New York: “Offering detailed information on the most commonly spoken languages at the citywide, borough and Community District levels, as well as statistics for additional language groups, the tool provides a powerful new way to examine the city’s rich linguistic diversity and better understand local language service needs.”

item.title: Discovery Center’s Historic Photo Archive online, open to public
item.description: Columbia Gorge News: “Columbia Gorge Discovery Center and Museum has restored their Historic Photo Archives online…Thanks to a grant from the City of The Dalles, the public now can view more than 30,600 images from the museum’s vast photo collection.”

item.title: Former Microsoft dev built a 2.5KB Notepad clone with zero AI features
item.description: TechSpot: “[Dave] Plummer is the man who claims to have created some major Windows features, including the original Task Manager application. Now, the YouTuber and retired developer shared his latest creation: a text editor named TinyRetroPad, which is designed to mimic Notepad’s text editing functionality while staying as small as possible on disk.”

item.title: VR and gaming are adding a kick to taekwondo
item.description: Associated Press: “Competitors wear VR headsets that transport them into a digital 3D arena, and strap motion-tracking sensors on their spine, thighs and shins. They use their bodies to control digital avatars in noncontact virtual matches, where every fast and well-timed strike depletes the opponent’s virtual health bar.”

item.title: Grim New Details From the Life of the Plaintiff in Social Media’s ‘Big Tobacco’ Case
item.description: Gizmodo: “K.G.M., the profile says, was a working class child of a fairly recent divorce when she started using YouTube, and was obsessed with her older sister who was careening toward an eating disorder. She was struggling in school. It’s familiar, and so is the idea of coping with heavy use of YouTube.”

item.title: $40 million for 9/11 document discovery, release included in city budget
item.description: The Chief: “The city will devote $34.2 million in the coming fiscal year to creating a public online portal to post documents related to post-9/11 air quality and health risks as part of the $125.8 billion Fiscal Year 2027 city budget announced June 30. Also included in the finalized budget is $6.25 million for the city’s Department of Investigation, $4 million of which will go towards completing the City Council-mandated inquiry into documents maintained by agencies across the city government from the period after 9/11.”

item.title: How a Twitter Post Discovered a New Wasp Species to Japan
item.description: Nautilus: “In 2018, insect enthusiast and author Kanji Toyosaki posted a photo to Twitter (now X) of a tiny wasp laying its eggs on a praying mantis’ egg case. The photo caught the attention of Japanese entomologist Taisuke Kawano of the Kyushu University Museum, who formally described the male of the species (Eupelmus curvator) for the first time in the journal Travaux du Muséum National d’Histoire Naturelle ‘Grigore Antipa.'”

item.title: Sound archive to be safeguarded thanks to university funding
item.description: Shropshire Council: “The collections include local radio archives, oral history interviews, and music recordings. The recordings frequently capture the memories and experiences of people and communities who are underrepresented in the archival record. They include memories of local industries, rural life, the natural world, and the experiences of people and communities who have made the Midlands their home. During the next year, an initial 1,200 recordings will be digitised and preserved. A range of events and learning activities will take place across the region, designed to showcase this important heritage.” Good afternoon, Internet…
